specPoints.text: know Hess’s Law and be able to apply it to: i constructing enthalpy cycles ii calculating enthalpy changes of reaction using data provided, or data selected from a table or obtained from experiments

primer.text: Enthalpy changes obey a route independence rule. Hess's law lets you build an energy cycle through intermediate elements or combustion steps and add the legs algebraically. This note constructs the two standard cycles - reaction from formation data, formation from combustion data - and works full numerical examples on both.

lessons.title: Hess's law and constructing cycles
sourceHeadings: Calculating ΔH<sub>r </sub>from ΔH<sub>f</sub> using Hess’s Law energy cycles
lessons.opening: Hess's law says the enthalpy change between reactants and products is fixed by the two levels, not by the route between them. That licence lets you build an energy cycle through any intermediate you can tabulate - usually the elements - and add the legs algebraically.
keyPoints: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken.
The direct route from reactants to products equals the sum of any indirect route's legs.
Energy cycles are drawn with the elements sitting on a common level as the intermediate.
Formation-route cycles point downward from elements to compounds; the arrows carry the tabulated values.
Adding the legs with correct signs recovers the enthalpy change the experiment cannot measure directly.

low.restatement: The enthalpy gap between reactants and products is one number no matter how you travel; draw the cycle, write the tabulated values on the arrows, and add them with the right signs.
low.analogy: Two routes up the same mountain gain the same altitude; the cycle is just the map that lists both routes' legs.
low.examPointer: Draw the cycle before calculating - the arrow directions carry the signs, and misdirected arrows are the standard error.

medium.restatement: The law works because enthalpy is a state function: only the state matters, not the path, so algebraic addition of legs through the elements cancels the intermediates and leaves the direct change.
medium.analogy: Altitude is a state function: your height above sea level never remembers which trail you took.
medium.examPointer: State the law in the words 'independent of the route taken' - paraphrases such as 'energy is conserved' score differently.

check.stem: What does Hess's law assert about an enthalpy change?

options.text: It is independent of the route taken between reactants and products
It depends on the route's speed
It changes when a catalyst is added
options.explanation: Catalysts move the hump, not the levels.

check.stem: On a formation-route energy cycle, where do the elements sit?

options.text: On their own level, joined to both reactants and products by arrows
options.explanation: The elements are the shared intermediate.
Elements and compounds occupy separate levels.
The elements are the whole point of the construction.

check.stem: Why can a reaction's enthalpy change be found from tabulated formation values?

options.text: Both reactants and products can be decomposed to the same elements on paper
options.explanation: The shared element level closes the cycle.

options.text: The law only holds for elements
options.explanation: The law holds for all routes.
Many are directly measurable; cycles cover the impossible ones.

check.stem: What must you track most carefully when adding the legs of a cycle?

options.text: The direction of each arrow, which fixes each sign
options.explanation: Reversed arrows flip the value's sign.

check.stem: Which phrase belongs in a full statement of Hess's law?

options.text: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken
Energy cannot be created or destroyed
options.explanation: That is the first law - true but not the Hess statement.

options.text: Reactions release energy in all routes

check.stem: State Hess's law in its standard wording.
check.modelAnswer: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken between reactants and products.

check.stem: Describe the construction of a simple energy cycle through the elements.
check.modelAnswer: Draw reactants and products on the top level, place the elements on a lower level, and join them with arrows carrying the tabulated formation values.

check.stem: Explain why enthalpy being a state function makes Hess's law work.
check.modelAnswer: A state function's value depends only on the current state, so any complete journey between the same two states accumulates the same net change, whatever the path - legs through elements are just one such path.

check.stem: A direct reaction's enthalpy change cannot be measured because the reaction is too slow. Explain how a cycle solves the problem.
check.modelAnswer: Choose tabulated intermediates (the elements), add the legs algebraically with arrow-directed signs, and the sum delivers the direct change without running the slow reaction.

lessons.title: Reaction enthalpy from formation data
sourceHeadings: Calculating ΔH<sub>r</sub> <sub> </sub>from ΔH<sub>f</sub> using Hess’s Law energy cycles
lessons.opening: With the elements as the common ground, the formation route collapses to one slogan: products minus reactants. Multiply each tabulated formation value by its equation's mole count, total the two sides, and subtract - the workhorse calculation of the chapter.
keyPoints: The formation route gives: enthalpy change of reaction = sum of formation values of products minus those of reactants.
Multiply every tabulated value by its coefficient in the reaction equation.
Elements in their standard states contribute zero, so they drop out of the sum.
The worked-example cycle runs the calculation stepwise: elements level, arrows, then the subtraction.
A positive result means the reaction is endothermic; negative means exothermic.

low.restatement: Add up the products' formation values, add up the reactants', and subtract reactants from products - remembering each value may need multiplying by its mole count.
low.analogy: A shopping bill: itemise the trolley (products), itemise the returned goods (reactants), and the net charge is the reaction's price.
low.examPointer: Show the multiplication step for coefficients above one - skipping it is the most common numerical fault in these calculations.

medium.restatement: The subtraction encodes the cycle's geometry: the reactants' leg climbs back up to the elements (reversing their formation, hence minus) and the products' leg descends (hence plus) - the slogan is the diagram written in algebra.
medium.analogy: Return then purchase: the refund (minus reactants) plus the new bill (plus products) nets the day's true cost.
medium.examPointer: Quote the final value with units kJ mol^-1 and its sign - the sign classifies the reaction and carries its own mark.

check.stem: The formation-route formula reads: enthalpy of reaction equals:

options.text: Sum of products' formation values minus sum of reactants' formation values
The larger side minus the smaller
options.explanation: The sides are fixed by the equation, not by size.

check.stem: Formation values of N2(g) and H2(g) appear in the ammonia cycle. What do they contribute?

options.text: Nothing - both are elements in their standard states

options.explanation: Bond enthalpies belong to a different route.

check.stem: A formation value must be multiplied when:

options.text: Its species' coefficient in the reaction equation exceeds one
Never - values are used as tabulated

check.stem: Ammonia synthesis: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 with formation value of NH3 at -46 kJ mol^-1. The reaction enthalpy is:

options.text: -92 kJ mol^-1, from 2 x (-46) minus zero
options.explanation: Two moles of ammonia form; the elements contribute zero.
The sign follows the products' negative value.

check.stem: A formation-route calculation returns +178 kJ mol^-1. Classify the reaction.

options.text: Impossible - enthalpy changes are always negative

options.explanation: The sign says nothing about catalysts.

check.stem: State the formation-route formula in words.
check.modelAnswer: The reaction's enthalpy change equals the sum of the products' formation values minus the sum of the reactants' formation values, each scaled by its coefficient.

check.stem: Compute the enthalpy change of N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g) given the formation value of NH3 as -46 kJ mol^-1.
check.modelAnswer: 2 x (-46) - (0 + 0) = -92 kJ mol^-1, so the synthesis is exothermic.

check.stem: Explain why the formation route works even when the reaction itself cannot be run in a calorimeter.
check.modelAnswer: The cycle never runs the actual reaction - it computes the same level gap through the elements' legs, so unmeasurable reactions still yield exact values from tabulated data.

check.stem: A formation-route calculation gives the reactants' total as -602 kJ and the products' total as -780 kJ. State the reaction's enthalpy change and its class.
check.modelAnswer: The change is (-780) - (-602) = -178 kJ mol-1, negative and therefore exothermic.

lessons.title: Formation enthalpy from combustion data
sourceHeadings: Calculating ΔH<sub>f</sub> from ΔH<sub>c </sub>using Hess’s Law energy cycles
lessons.opening: When formation values are unmeasurable, combustion values usually are not - every substance burns. The combustion cycle flips the slogan: the target compound's formation value equals the reactant elements' combustions minus the compound's own combustion.
keyPoints: The combustion route gives: formation value of the target = sum of reactant elements' combustion values minus the target's combustion value.
Combustion arrows point downward from every species to the shared combustion products level.
The target compound's combustion leg runs the wrong way for formation, hence the subtraction flips its sign.
The worked example prices propan-1-ol from carbon, hydrogen and the compound's own combustion.
Watch the stoichiometry: each element's combustion must be multiplied by its mole count.

low.restatement: Everything burns down to the same products level: the elements' burns added together, minus the compound's own burn, equals the formation value you could never measure directly.
low.analogy: Three slides into the same swimming pool: two start from the elements' platform, one from the compound's - the compound's platform height is the difference of the slide lengths.
low.examPointer: The compound's combustion value enters with a plus after the minus in the bracket - writing it as minus twice is the standard slip.

medium.restatement: The sign flip is cycle geometry: formation climbs from elements up to the compound, but combustion descends from the compound, so its tabulated negative value enters the sum reversed - the algebra is the ladder read in both directions.
medium.analogy: Measuring a shelf's height by how far it is above the floor (formation) versus how far below the ceiling it hangs (combustion) - one reading flips into the other.
medium.examPointer: Check the mole counts before subtracting: 3 carbons means 3 combustions of carbon, each carrying its own tabulated value.

check.stem: The combustion-route formula for a formation value reads:

options.text: Elements' combustions summed, minus the compound's combustion
Elements' combustions plus the compound's combustion
Half the sum of all combustions

check.stem: Why do all combustion arrows converge on one level?

options.text: Every substance burns to the same oxides - carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: The shared products level closes the cycle.
The chemistry dictates the level, not the table.

options.text: Water and carbon dioxide are elements

check.stem: Combustion values: C(s) -394, H2(g) -286, CH3COCH3(l) -1821 (kJ mol^-1). The formation value of propanone, C3H6O, is:

options.explanation: 3 carbons and 3 hydrogens burn, then the compound's burn flips.
That adds everything without the flip.
The result is negative - formation from elements is exothermic here.
That counts only the carbon leg.

check.stem: In the propanone cycle, why does hydrogen's combustion enter three times?

options.explanation: Each mole of hydrogen burns once.
It holds eight; the coefficient counts moles of H2.
Oxygen's combustion is not part of the leg.

check.stem: Why is the combustion route preferred when formation values are unavailable?

options.text: Combustions are readily measurable for nearly every substance
options.explanation: Burning is easy; synthesising from elements may be impossible.
The route's virtue is measurability, not simplicity.

check.stem: State the combustion-route formula for a formation value in words.
check.modelAnswer: The formation value equals the summed combustion values of the reactant elements minus the combustion value of the target compound itself.

check.stem: Compute the formation value of propanone given combustion values C(s) -394, H2(g) -286 and CH3COCH3(l) -1821 kJ mol^-1.
Explain why the compound's own combustion value enters the sum with a reversed effect.
check.modelAnswer: Formation climbs from elements up to the compound while combustion descends from it, so the compound's leg runs opposite to the cycle's direction and its tabulated value enters effectively flipped.

check.stem: Verify the propanone formation calculation arithmetically: 3(-394), 3(-286) and -(-1821).
check.modelAnswer: 3 x 394 = 1182, 3 x 286 = 858, so the sum is -1182 - 858 + 1821 = -219 kJ mol^-1, matching the tabulated cycle answer.

glossary.definition: The rule that a reaction's enthalpy change is independent of the route taken between reactants and products.
A diagram routing reactants and products through a shared intermediate level whose legs sum to the direct change.
The cycle through the elements that yields a reaction's enthalpy from tabulated formation values.
The cycle through the combustion products level that yields a formation value from tabulated combustion values.

workedExample.prompt: Given combustion enthalpies C(s) = -394, H2(g) = -286 and C3H7OH(l) = -1821 kJ mol^-1, calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of propan-1-ol.
steps: Place the combustion products (CO2 and H2O) on the shared lower level.
Sum the elements' combustions: 3 x (-394) + 4 x (-286) = -1182 - 1144 = -2326 kJ.
Reverse the compound's own combustion: -(-1821) = +1821 kJ.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The standard enthalpy change of formation of propan-1-ol is -505 kJ mol^-1.
